verses.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” So Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense.
“I consider myself fortunate, King Agrippa, to make my defense before you today against all the charges the Jews bring against me,
especially because you know all the Jewish customs and disputes. So please listen to me patiently.
“All the Jews know how I lived from my youth, from the beginning among my own people and in Jerusalem.
They’ve known me for a long time. If they’re willing to testify, they know I lived as a Pharisee, the strictest group in our religion.
Now I’m standing trial because I hope in the promise God made to our ancestors.
Our twelve tribes hope to receive that promise as they worship God earnestly day and night. It’s because of this hope, King Agrippa, that the Jews accuse me!
Why should any of you find it impossible to believe that God raises the dead?
“I myself was convinced I should oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth in every way.
That’s what I did in Jerusalem. With authority from the chief priests, I locked many of God’s people in prison. When they were sentenced to death, I voted against them.
I often punished them in the synagogues and tried to force them to blaspheme. I was so furious with them that I chased them down even in foreign cities.
“That’s how I came to Damascus, with authority and a commission from the chief priests.
At noon, King Agrippa, I saw a light from heaven brighter than the sun shining around me and those traveling with me.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice speaking to me in Hebrew: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It’s hard for you to kick against the goads.’
I asked, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, the one you’re persecuting.
Get up and stand on your feet. I’ve appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as my servant and witness to what you’ve seen and what I’ll show you.
I’ll rescue you from your own people and from the Gentiles. I’m sending you to them
to open their eyes, so they may turn from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God. Then they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those made holy through faith in me.’
“So, King Agrippa, I didn’t disobey the vision from heaven.
I preached first in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout Judea, and also to the Gentiles. I told them to repent and turn to God, and to show that change by how they live.
That’s why the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
But God has helped me, and to this day I stand here testifying to everyone, both ordinary people and important ones. I’m saying nothing beyond what Moses and the Prophets said would happen:
that the Christ would suffer, and that by rising from the dead he would be the first to announce light to our people and to the Gentiles.”
As Paul said this in his defense, Festus shouted, “Paul, you’re out of your mind! All your learning is making you crazy!”
Paul replied, “I’m not crazy, most excellent Festus. I’m speaking words that are true and sensible.
The king knows about these things, and I can speak freely to him. I’m sure none of this has escaped his notice, because it didn’t happen in some hidden corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the Prophets? I know you do.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “Do you think you can persuade me so quickly to become a Christian?”
Paul answered, “Quickly or not, I pray to God that not only you but everyone listening to me today would become like me—except for these chains.”
The king stood up, along with the governor, Bernice, and the others sitting with them.
After they left, they said to each other, “This man hasn’t done anything deserving death or imprisonment.”
Agrippa told Festus, “This man could have been released if he hadn’t appealed to Caesar.”
